- Coherent, one random offset: each sample is treated as a hard square spot of side $s=R\times0.0036^\circ$ (the 250 m confocal 1/e² half-angle from the table above, so the 1/e² radius is used as the side). The fraction of grid offsets for which it overlaps the object is $P_1=\min[1,(W+s)/p]\,\min[1,(H+s)/p]$. For 10 × 10 cm at 250 m, $s=1.57$ cm and $P_1=(11.57/21.8)^2=0.28$; for 20 × 15 cm at 200 m, $s=1.26$ cm, $p=17.45$ cm and $P_1=1\times16.26/17.45=0.93$.

edits.new:
- Coherent, one random offset: the two binary rules of §C10.3b, Result 4, applied to the 20 mm collimated beam, whose 1/e² radius $w$ is 1.22, 1.42 and 1.64 cm at 150, 200 and 250 m. The lower value counts an overlap when the beam centre lands inside the object, $\min(1,W/p)\min(1,H/p)$. The upper value counts one when the 1/e² circle touches the object, i.e. when the centre lands inside the object grown by $w$ on every side, of area $WH+2w(W+H)+\pi w^2$, with a grown side that exceeds the pitch capped at one pitch. For 10 × 10 cm at 250 m, $(10/21.8)^2=0.21$ and $(100+65.6+8.5)\ {\rm cm^2}/476\ {\rm cm^2}=0.37$. For 15 × 10 cm at 150 m the grown width, 17.4 cm, exceeds the 13.1 cm pitch, so the upper value is $(10+2.4)/13.1=0.95$.
- Five independent offsets: the chance that at least one of five frames overlaps, $1-(1-P_1)^5$, where $P_1$ is the one-offset fraction, e.g. $1-0.79^5=0.69$ and $1-0.63^5=0.90$.

edits.old: - **Sunlight can favour coherent detection.** In a background-limited direct detector with fixed angular acceptance and integration time, signal and solar background both grow with aperture, so the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) scales approximately as $\sqrt{A_{\rm rx}}$. A larger aperture can also increase SPAD pile-up: after each detection a SPAD is blind for a dead time, so strong light saturates it and biases the timing. A narrowband LO receiver strongly rejects broadband sunlight, though it is not literally background-free; its aperture scaling still depends on beam propagation, mode overlap and noise regime.
edits.new: - **Sunlight can favour coherent detection.** For SPAD ToF, bright sun costs mainly dead time and pile-up rather than per-bin signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) (§C6(d)): after each detection a SPAD is blind for a dead time, so background light both hides returns and biases the timing. In a fully sunlit scene this cuts the effective PDE by about a third at 940 nm behind a 10 nm filter, and by three-quarters or more at 905 nm behind 20–40 nm filters (§C6(d); §C7a's central case uses a live fraction of 0.784), and a larger aperture collects proportionally more background. Only for a purely background-limited detector, with fixed angular acceptance and integration time, does SNR scale as $\sqrt{A_{\rm rx}}$. A narrowband LO receiver strongly rejects broadband sunlight (about $10^3$ photons/s in one mode, §C6(d′)), though it is not literally background-free; its aperture scaling still depends on beam propagation, mode overlap and noise regime.
edits.why: Describes the mechanism the report's ToF model uses (dead time and pile-up), per §C6(d).
